hook.headline: You will die. Now what?
hook.body: One fact is unusually stubborn: your life ends. aBit’s Death path doesn’t flinch from that. It asks what mortality means for persons, time, value, and how to live before the lights go out.

stakes.headline: What’s on the table
stakes.body: Is death the end—or only a change of address? Would forever be a gift or a trap? What is dying, exactly? The course splits metaphysics (what we are) from value theory (what makes death bad, and life good).

final.prompt: Across the arc—from persons and dualism to deprivation, immortality, fear, and suicide—what is Death ultimately asking you to hold?
final.correct: What death means for persons, value, and how to live given mortality.
distractors: How to perform clinical resuscitations in detail.
A survey of campus parking rules.
Whether Yale’s dining halls serve dessert.
final.explanation: Across dualism, identity, deprivation, immortality, fear, and suicide, the arc is philosophical: what we are, why death matters, how to live.

hook.headline: Drawing the map
hook.body: Kagan sets the syllabus like a border treaty: philosophical questions about death are in; medical trivia and grief counseling are out. First half: what persons and death are. Second half: whether death is bad—and what follows.

key_term.headline: Two halves
key_term.body: Metaphysics asks what must be true for someone to die. Value theory asks why that matters. Keep the split in mind; arguments will bounce between them all term.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Treat every later lecture as answering either “What is going on?” or “Why should I care?” If you lose the thread, return to that fork.

quiz.prompt: What does Kagan say the course will emphasize?
quiz.correct: Philosophical questions that arise when we contemplate death’s nature.
distractors: Clinical procedures for declaring someone dead in hospitals.
A history of funeral customs across cultures only.
How to write a living will step by step.
quiz.explanation: The opening frames Death as philosophy—metaphysics then value—not medicine or etiquette.

2.title: The Nature of Persons: Dualism vs. Physicalism

hook.headline: What is a person?
hook.body: Before death can matter, we need a subject. Dualism says you are body plus soul. Physicalism says you are a body—though a body with remarkable powers of thought and action.

key_term.headline: Dualism
key_term.body: On the dualist picture, something non-physical rides along with the organism. That “soul” is often cast as what thinks, chooses, and maybe survives the corpse.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Notice how each later argument about souls, identity, or immortality quietly picks a side in this fight—or tries to dissolve it.

quiz.prompt: How does physicalism answer “What is a person?”
quiz.correct: A person is just a body—with a rich set of abilities.
distractors: A person is only an immortal soul with no body.
A person is whatever society labels as such this week.
A person is a legal fiction with no metaphysical claim.
quiz.explanation: Physicalism rejects an extra soul-stuff; the person is the capable body itself.

3.title: Arguments for the Existence of the Soul, Part I

hook.headline: Invisible posits
hook.body: Why believe in a soul you can’t see? One strategy: inference to the best explanation. We invent unseen furniture when it best accounts for what we already agree happens.

key_term.headline: Best explanation
key_term.body: If ordinary matter can’t easily explain minds, meaning, or unity of consciousness, dualists say a soul is the cleaner story—debate whether that claim holds.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Ask of every soul argument: what exactly is being explained, and is the soul doing unique work—or just renaming the mystery?

quiz.prompt: What is an “inference to the best explanation” doing here?
quiz.correct: Positing unseen things to explain agreed-upon phenomena.
distractors: Proving souls by quoting scripture alone.
Measuring brain waves to locate the soul organ.
Defining death legally in every state.
quiz.explanation: The lecture’s first family of soul arguments works by explanatory inference, not direct sighting.

4.title: Introduction to Plato's Phaedo; Arguments for the Existence of the Soul, Part II

hook.headline: Enter Phaedo
hook.body: Plato’s dialogue stages Socrates on the day of his death—talking souls while facing his own. Kagan uses it to gather more dualist ammo, especially free will.

key_term.headline: Free will lever
key_term.body: Dualists often claim: if we truly choose, we can’t be only physical machines. A soul is wheeled in to host that freedom.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Watch whether free will really requires non-physical stuff—or whether the dualist smuggles in a contested picture of choice.

quiz.prompt: Why do dualists bring free will into the soul debate?
quiz.correct: They argue free will can’t fit a purely physical person, so a soul is needed.
distractors: They think free will is impossible for souls too.
They only care about free will in corporate law.
They use free will to prove the body is immortal.
quiz.explanation: Free will is framed as an objection to pure physicalism that motivates belief in an immaterial soul.

5.title: Arguments for the Existence of the Soul, Part III: Free Will and Near-Death Experiences

hook.headline: Three premises
hook.body: The free-will argument tightens: (1) we have free will; (2) nothing determined has free will; (3) pure physical systems are determined. Conclusion: we aren’t purely physical.

key_term.headline: Determinism
key_term.body: If every physical event is fixed by prior causes, and you are only physics, your “choices” look like falling dominoes. Dualists refuse that picture for persons.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: You can reject the conclusion by denying a premise—deny free will, deny that physics implies determinism, or deny that free will needs indeterminacy.

quiz.prompt: What conclusion does the free-will triad aim at?
quiz.correct: Humans are not a purely physical system.
distractors: All animals lack free will entirely.
Near-death experiences prove reincarnation.
Determinism only applies to stars, not brains.
quiz.explanation: From free will + anti-determinism + physical determinism, dualists infer we aren’t only physical.

6.title: Arguments for the Existence of the Soul, Part IV; Plato, Part I

hook.headline: Cartesian cracks, Platonic realms
hook.body: Cartesian soul arguments show wear. Plato offers another metaphysics: besides the changing empirical world, there is a second realm of stable Forms.

key_term.headline: Two realms
key_term.body: The everyday world is messy and temporary. Forms are the clean, intelligible originals—Justice itself, Equality itself—that minds somehow grasp.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: If Forms aren’t physical, grasping them may require a non-physical grasper. That’s the bridge Plato builds toward soul.

quiz.prompt: What key Platonic idea does Kagan highlight here?
quiz.correct: Besides the empirical world, there is a second realm of Forms.
distractors: Only atoms exist and Forms are illusions.
Souls are identical to left-hemisphere activity.
Death is purely a legal category.
quiz.explanation: The lecture pivots into Plato’s two-realm metaphysics as setup for soul arguments.

7.title: Plato, Part II: Arguments for the Immortality of the Soul

hook.headline: Grasping the Forms
hook.body: If Forms are non-physical, a body alone can’t know them. Plato’s “argument from the nature of the forms” says the soul must be what understands that higher realm.

key_term.headline: Argument from the Forms
key_term.body: Knowledge of timeless objects seems to demand a knower that isn’t stuck in flesh. Immortality often rides along with that claim.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Ask whether understanding abstract truths really needs a separable soul—or whether brains can track patterns without extra ontology.

quiz.prompt: What does the argument from the nature of the Forms claim?
quiz.correct: Non-physical Forms must be grasped by a non-physical soul, not the body.
distractors: Forms are physical objects stored in temples.
Only children can know Forms.
Forms prove the body is immortal by itself.
quiz.explanation: Plato links grasp of non-physical Forms to a soul capable of knowing them.

8.title: Plato, Part III: Arguments for the Immortality of the Soul (cont.)

hook.headline: Simple things don’t shatter
hook.body: Plato’s “argument from simplicity”: destruction means taking something apart. If the soul has no parts, it can’t be dismantled—so it can’t die that way.

key_term.headline: Simplicity
key_term.body: A composite can break. A partless soul, on this story, has nothing to unscrew. Immortality follows if that picture is right.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Challenge both claims: Is the soul really simple? And is every destruction a matter of parts coming loose?

quiz.prompt: What does Plato’s argument from simplicity say about destruction?
quiz.correct: To be destroyed, something must have parts that can be taken apart.
distractors: Only heavy objects can be destroyed.
Destruction requires divine permission only.
Anything simple is automatically physical.
quiz.explanation: Simplicity is used to block the usual path to destruction—disassembly into parts.

9.title: Plato, Part IV: Arguments for the Immortality of the Soul (cont.)

hook.headline: Essential properties
hook.body: Kagan presses simplicity further: changeless, partless, indestructible. Then comes the “argument from essential properties”—what the soul essentially is may rule out death.

key_term.headline: Essential properties
key_term.body: If life or thought belongs to the soul’s essence, then a “dead soul” is a contradiction—like a square circle—rather than a sad event.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Essential-property moves are powerful—and slippery. Watch whether Plato defines the soul so that immortality is baked in by vocabulary.

quiz.prompt: What is distinctive about the argument from essential properties?
quiz.correct: It claims the soul’s essence includes features that make death impossible for it.
distractors: It measures soul weight on ancient scales.
It proves only animals have souls.
It shows Forms are destroyed each evening.
quiz.explanation: The argument turns on what must be true of a soul by nature, not on empirical survival stories.

10.title: Personal Identity, Part I: Identity Across Space and Time and the Soul Theory

hook.headline: Same person tomorrow?
hook.body: Metaphysical key to personal identity: what makes you now the same you later? The soul theory answers: same soul, same person—wherever the body goes.

key_term.headline: Soul theory
key_term.body: Identity rides on an inner nugget that persists. Bodies may swap; memories may blur; the soul is the ticket that keeps “you” continuous.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: If the soul is undetectable, how do we ever know we’ve got the same one? That epistemic headache drives rival theories next.

quiz.prompt: On the soul theory, what makes you the same person over time?
quiz.correct: Having the same soul.
distractors: Wearing the same clothes.
Living in the same city.
Sharing a name on a passport alone.
quiz.explanation: Soul theory locates identity in persistence of the same soul across time.

11.title: Personal Identity, Part II: The Body Theory and the Personality Theory

hook.headline: Body or biography?
hook.body: Two rivals: the body view ties identity to the same living organism; the personality view ties it to the ongoing pattern of beliefs, desires, memories, and projects.

key_term.headline: Personality view
key_term.body: You are your psychological profile in motion. Swap brains or upload minds, and identity may travel with the pattern—not the meat.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Science-fiction thought experiments will pressure both views. Notice which intuition you trust when body and personality split.

quiz.prompt: What does the personality view treat as the key to identity?
quiz.correct: A unique ongoing set of beliefs, desires, memories, and goals.
distractors: Only DNA sequence with no psychology.
Social security number alone.
The soul as a glowing orb.
quiz.explanation: Personality theory identifies persons via continuing psychological profile.

12.title: Personal Identity, Part III: Objections to the Personality Theory

hook.headline: The duplication problem
hook.body: If personality can be copied, two later people might share your pattern. Both can’t be uniquely you—so bare psychological continuity looks incomplete.

key_term.headline: Branching
key_term.body: When one past person “splits” into two equally good continuers, identity talk breaks. Theories need a no-branching clause—or a new question.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Duplication doesn’t just threaten personality theory; it forces every identity story to say what happens when there are too many heirs.

quiz.prompt: What is the main objection raised against the personality theory here?
quiz.correct: The problem of duplication—two copies can’t both be uniquely you.
distractors: Personalities never change at all.
Bodies cannot age.
Memories are always false.
quiz.explanation: Duplication cases show psychological continuity can fork, undermining unique identity.

13.title: Personal Identity, Part IV: What Matters?

hook.headline: No branching, then what matters
hook.body: Personality theory is patched: same personality without branching. Similar patches hit other views. Then Kagan shifts: maybe “what matters in survival” isn’t strict identity.

key_term.headline: What matters
key_term.body: Care about future experiences continuous with yours—even if metaphysics won’t crown a single identical continuer. Survival-value can peel apart from identity.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: When death debates heat up, ask whether we fear losing identity itself—or losing the goods that a continuer would enjoy.

quiz.prompt: How is the personality theory revised in this lecture?
quiz.correct: Same personality counts only if there is no branching or duplication.
distractors: Personality is abandoned entirely for soul theory.
Only body continuity matters forever after.
Identity requires identical fingerprints only.
quiz.explanation: A no-branching requirement is added so personality continuity can’t fork into two “yous.”

14.title: What Matters (cont.); The Nature of Death, Part I

hook.headline: From survival to dying
hook.body: Maybe survival means a future someone with a personality like yours. Then the camera turns: what is it to die? Focus falls on bodily and mental functions that mark the moment.

key_term.headline: Functions
key_term.body: Death isn’t just a calendar date. It’s tied to the collapse of capacities—circulation, respiration, cognition—that keep a person going.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Defining death is partly scientific and partly philosophical: which functions are essential to still being here?

quiz.prompt: When defining the moment of death, what does Kagan first emphasize?
quiz.correct: Bodily and mental functions crucial to marking death.
distractors: Only the opinion of distant relatives.
Astrology charts for the day of death.
Whether the person owned property.
quiz.explanation: The turn to “what is it to die?” begins with the functions that fail at death.

15.title: The Nature of Death (cont.); Believing You Will Die

hook.headline: When P-functions stop
hook.body: Stopping person-functions looks like death—but sleep and coma are exceptions that force finer distinctions. Then a psychological twist: on some level, nobody quite believes they’ll die.

key_term.headline: Disbelief
key_term.body: We can recite mortality while living as if the end is always for someone else. That gap between saying and believing will power later ethics and fear.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: A clean definition of death still leaves the human habit of denying it. Both threads matter for the badness of death.

quiz.prompt: Why isn’t “stopping person-functions” a complete definition of death by itself?
quiz.correct: Exceptions like sleep or coma show temporary non-functioning isn’t always death.
distractors: Because death never involves the body.
Because functions never stop in living things.
Because only plants have person-functions.
quiz.explanation: Sleep and coma show we need a more careful account than mere temporary loss of function.

16.title: Dying Alone; The Badness of Death, Part I

hook.headline: Ivan Ilych’s shock
hook.body: Tolstoy’s Ilych knew death was coming yet never believed it—until illness made mortality personal. Kagan treats him as ordinary: abstract knowledge, concrete denial.

key_term.headline: Sudden intimacy
key_term.body: Death becomes real when it stops being a statistic and starts being your schedule. That conversion is part of why death feels uniquely bad.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: When we ask why death is bad, notice whether we’re talking about the state of being dead—or the rupture of finally believing it.

quiz.prompt: What does Ilych illustrate about typical attitudes toward mortality?
quiz.correct: People can know death is coming yet not really believe it until it becomes personal.
distractors: Everyone constantly meditates on their death date.
Only aristocrats fear death.
Illness never changes how we think about dying.
quiz.explanation: Ilych models abstract acknowledgment paired with practical disbelief—until crisis.

17.title: The Badness of Death, Part II: The Deprivation Account

hook.headline: Missing the goods
hook.body: On the deprivation account, death is bad because it cuts off the good things life would have continued to offer. Being dead isn’t a painful experience—it’s a comparative loss.

key_term.headline: Deprivation
key_term.body: You’re worse off by missing future joys, projects, and loves—not by suffering inside the grave. Badness is about lost opportunity.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: If deprivation is the story, earlier death can be worse than later death because more possible goods get canceled.

quiz.prompt: According to the deprivation account, why is death bad?
quiz.correct: Because it deprives you of the good things continued life would bring.
distractors: Because being dead feels constantly painful.
Because funerals are expensive.
Because death increases your future pleasures.
quiz.explanation: Deprivation locates badness in lost goods, not in an experienced hell of being dead.

18.title: The Badness of Death, Part III; Immortality, Part I

hook.headline: Prenatal nonexistence & forever
hook.body: If missing future life is bad, is missing life before birth also bad? Nagel, Feldman, Parfit enter. Then the pivot: would immortality actually be desirable?

key_term.headline: Asymmetry
key_term.body: Many feel future deprivation hurts while past nonexistence doesn’t. Explaining that asymmetry is a live puzzle for deprivation theorists.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Wanting endless life is not automatic. The next lectures ask under what conditions forever would still be a life worth wanting.

quiz.prompt: After discussing deprivation, what new question does Kagan raise?
quiz.correct: Whether immortality would be desirable, and under what conditions.
distractors: How to build cryonics tanks in the lab.
Whether insects fear death.
How to rename the course mid-semester.
quiz.explanation: The lecture moves from badness puzzles into the desirability of living forever.

19.title: Immortality Part II; The Value of Life, Part I

hook.headline: Forever—and what makes life good
hook.body: Would endless life stay desirable under the right conditions? Then: what makes a life worth living at all? Hedonism says pleasure—until the “experience machine” thought experiment pushes back.

key_term.headline: Experience machine
key_term.body: If you could plug into perfect simulated joys, would you? Many refuse—suggesting we value contact with reality, not pleasure alone.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Your theory of well-being shapes whether immortality looks like paradise or a polished trap.

quiz.prompt: What challenge does the experience machine pose to hedonism?
quiz.correct: It suggests we care about more than pleasure—like real connection to the world.
distractors: It proves pleasure is the only good.
It shows machines cannot simulate joy.
It argues immortality is always good.
quiz.explanation: Refusal to plug in is used against the idea that pleasure exhausts well-being.

20.title: The Value of Life, Part II; Other Bad Aspects of Death, Part I

hook.headline: Containers of value
hook.body: Neutral container theory: life’s value is just the sum of pleasant and painful contents. Valuable container theory: being alive itself adds worth beyond the playlist of moments.

key_term.headline: Valuable container
key_term.body: Existence isn’t a blank vessel. Merely living may carry value—so death can rob you of the container, not only of what’s inside.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: How you score the container changes how tragic early death looks—and how you weigh immortality.

quiz.prompt: How does the valuable container theory differ from the neutral container theory?
quiz.correct: It assigns value to being alive itself, not only to life’s pleasant or painful contents.
distractors: It denies that pleasure ever matters.
It claims only pain has value.
It treats life as worthless in every case.
quiz.explanation: Valuable container adds intrinsic worth to living; neutral container tallies only contents.

21.title: Other Bad Aspects of Death, Part II

hook.headline: Death can strike anywhere
hook.body: Ubiquity: death may come at any time, to anyone. Imagine death-free vacations or safe hours—then feel how much of life’s texture is shaped by that constant exposure.

key_term.headline: Ubiquity
key_term.body: The badness isn’t only deprivation at the end; it’s living under an open-ended threat that can cancel plans without warning.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: The human condition is life followed by death. Valuing that package—or resenting it—will steer how we fear and how we choose.

quiz.prompt: What does “ubiquity” add to the badness of death?
quiz.correct: Death may occur at any time and strike anyone—an open-ended exposure.
distractors: Death only happens on Tuesdays.
Death is rare and always predicted years ahead.
Only celebrities face sudden death.
quiz.explanation: Ubiquity highlights unpredictability and universal exposure, not just the final moment.

hook.headline: When fear makes sense
hook.body: How should thoughts of death shape a life? Fear can be fitting—or confused. Separate fear of dying (the process) from fear of being dead (the state and aftermath).

key_term.headline: Two fears
key_term.body: Pain, loss of control, and farewell belong to dying. Annihilation or the unknown belong to death itself. Different remedies fit different fears.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Before judging fear as irrational, name the object. Some fears track real losses; others may dissolve under clearer metaphysics.

quiz.prompt: What distinction does Kagan emphasize about fear?
quiz.correct: Fear of the process of dying versus fear of death itself and what may follow.
distractors: Fear of cats versus fear of dogs.
Fear only of public speaking.
Fear that grades will be too high.
quiz.explanation: The lecture separates dying-as-process from death-as-state when assessing appropriate fear.

23.title: How to Live Given the Certainty of Death

hook.headline: Finite time, chosen aims
hook.body: Knowing the story ends, how should you set goals and chase them? Time scarcity isn’t only a mood—it constrains which projects can even be sane.

key_term.headline: Time constraints
key_term.body: Ambitions that need centuries may be beautiful fantasies. Mortality pressures us toward scaled aims—and sharper tradeoffs.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Quality of life partly depends on matching projects to a mortal schedule instead of pretending you have infinite runway.

quiz.prompt: What practical question does this lecture press?
quiz.correct: How to set and pursue goals given that life will certainly end.
distractors: How to avoid ever thinking about goals.
How to live as if immortal without reflection.
How to outsource all choices to chance alone.
quiz.explanation: Certainty of death becomes a constraint on planning and the quality of a lived life.

24.title: Suicide, Part I: The Rationality of Suicide

hook.headline: Two lenses
hook.body: Suicide is explored under rationality (when ending life could make sense) and morality (when, if ever, it could be justified). Keep the lenses distinct.

key_term.headline: Rationality vs morality
key_term.body: A choice might be prudent for the agent yet still wrong—or kind yet self-destructive. The course examines both questions without collapsing them.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Graphs of life’s quality over time will appear next; they’re tools for the rationality question, not automatic moral verdicts.

quiz.prompt: What two contexts does Kagan use to explore suicide?
quiz.correct: Rationality (when it makes sense) and morality (when it can be justified).
distractors: Fashion and cuisine only.
Sports rankings and weather.
Typography and architecture.
quiz.explanation: The series opens by separating prudential and moral evaluations of ending one’s life.

25.title: Suicide, Part II: Deciding under Uncertainty

hook.headline: Choosing without a crystal ball
hook.body: More cases and graphs: when might ending life be rational? The hard part is deciding whether to continue when you can’t know how the future quality curve will bend.

key_term.headline: Uncertainty
key_term.body: Tomorrow’s pain or relief isn’t guaranteed. Rational choice under mortality must weigh unknown upturns, not only today’s trough.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: Even if deprivation and well-being theories are clear, uncertainty about your own future complicates any real decision procedure.

quiz.prompt: What complicates decisions about continuing or ending life in this lecture?
quiz.correct: You cannot be certain how future life quality will go.
distractors: Everyone knows their exact future happiness score.
Graphs make uncertainty disappear completely.
Only other people face uncertain futures.
quiz.explanation: Uncertainty about future well-being is central to the decision problem.

26.title: Suicide, Part III: The Morality of Suicide and Course Conclusion

hook.headline: Consequences—and duties
hook.body: Suicide’s effects on the agent and on others matter. Utilitarians may stop there; deontologists ask whether further moral constraints apply beyond outcomes.

key_term.headline: Deontology vs utility
key_term.body: If only consequences count, the math of harm and benefit decides. If rights or duties count too, some acts may be wrong even when the spreadsheet looks tidy.

takeaway.headline: Carry this forward
takeaway.body: The course closes where it began: death forces metaphysics and ethics into the same room. Your answers reshape how you live the time before it.

quiz.prompt: Besides consequences, what do deontologists say may matter morally about suicide?
quiz.correct: Further moral factors—such as duties or constraints—beyond outcomes alone.
distractors: Only the weather on the day of the act.
Nothing else; only taste in music.
Whether the person liked philosophy class.
quiz.explanation: The finale contrasts utilitarian consequence-counting with deontological constraints.
